contributions.headingText: Adenoid cystic carcinoma (AdCC) of the skin is a rare, malignant neoplasm histologically identical to homonymous tumours in the salivary gland and other glandular tissues.
2C33 & XH4302 Adnexal carcinoma of skin & Adenoid cystic carcinoma

The most common location is the scalp (affected in ~30% of cases), followed by the trunk (in particular the chest wall) and abdomen, which are affected in about 25% of cases. Other locations are rare {3010759}.

Patients with AdCC present with a solitary nodule averaging 30 mm (range: 5–80 mm), often present for several years before diagnosis. Pain and hyperaesthesia have rarely been reported with skin tumours {6326693}.

An incidence rate of 0.23 cases per 1 million person-years has been reported {20447723}. This neoplasm generally affects middle-aged to elderly individuals (average age: ~60 years). There is a slight female predilection (M:F ratio: 1:1.5).

About 60% of AdCCs harbour MYB gene activations, either through MYB chromosomal abnormalities or (less commonly) by MYB::NFIB fusion {27859477}. The MYB::NFIB fusion oncogene, which results from the recurrent chromosomal translocation t(6;9)(q22-23;p23-24), activates the transcription of genes involved in cell-cycle control, DNA repair, and apoptosis. The t(6;9) translocation appears to be tumour-type–specific; it has been identified in AdCCs arising in various anatomical locations {26076064}. In rare cases, alterations of the MYBL1 gene have been found {29570128; 30640762}.
AdCC is a poorly circumscribed, firm, solid mass that is tan, grey, or white, without necrosis and/or haemorrhage in most cases.

AdCCs are characterized by a mixture of cribriform, tubular, and solid patterns forming variably shaped nodules in the dermis and/or subcutis. The essential diagnostic feature is the coexistence of true small bilayered ducts and pseudocysts. The true ductal structures are usually sparse, have small round lumina, and are composed of inner epithelial cells with uniform round nuclei (sometimes with small nucleoli) surrounded by an outer layer of basal/myoepithelial cells. Intraluminal secretion can be seen. The pseudocystic structures are usually larger than ducts, and they contain abundant basophilic mucinous material that stains positively with Alcian blue at pH 2.5 and/or hyalinized eosinophilic material that gives a positive PAS reaction. The pseudocysts are often surrounded on the luminal edge by a thin layer of hyalinized connective tissue. The solid areas are composed of small basaloid cells with hyperchromatic, slightly angulated nuclei and scant cytoplasm. Mitotic activity is typically low in AdCC, and cellular pleomorphism is usually not a feature, although rare cases with high-grade atypia have been reported {24025525}. Perineural invasion is a common feature, whereas intraneural invasion is rare. The stroma is hyalinized and paucicellular. Occasional tumours display myxoid change, and fibrosis may be seen. Rare changes include cystic alteration, papillary formation, “spilling” or “pinching off” of epithelial or myoepithelial cells into a prominent myxoid stroma, and high-grade transformation {32732690; 34519081}.

Immunohistochemistry

The neoplastic cells show diffuse cytoplasmic positivity for broad-spectrum keratins, CAM5.2, and CK7. Staining with CK5/6 and D2-40 is variable. The basaloid and myoepithelial cells display nuclear staining for SOX10. EMA, CEA, and CK15 label the luminal cells surrounding the true ducts. The myoepithelial component is highlighted by staining for SMA, p63, and calponin. Most tumours express MYB, and all tumours are positive for KIT (CD117) {28098399; 26076064}.

Differential diagnosis

Cutaneous secretory carcinoma consists of back-to-back tubules and microcysts with conspicuous intraluminal secretions and shows a distinctive positivity for S100, mammaglobin, STAT5A, and NTRK {27631515}. Adenoid basal cell carcinoma is distinguished from AdCC by its lack of true ductal structures with myoepithelial cells, the presence of peripheral palisading of neoplastic cells and retraction artefact (often associated with stromal mucin), and at least focal areas of conventional basal cell carcinoma {3010759}. Cribriform carcinoma is composed of more eosinophilic cells; lacks myoepithelial cells; and focally manifests solid areas and peculiar thin, thread-like intraluminal bridging strands {21315957; 19751882}. Rare cases of spiradenoma and spiradenocylindroma display areas resembling AdCC by virtue of a cribriform pattern; homogeneous, eosinophilic, or granular basophilic material; and/or ductal structures with a recognizable peripheral myoepithelial cell layer. The proportion of the AdCC-like pattern varies from 5% to 30% of the tumour volume; therefore, the identification of typical areas of spiradenoma/cylindroma, as well as the absence of nuclear pleomorphism, perineural growth, and increased mitotic activity, facilitates the recognition of this spiradenoma/spiradenocylindroma with an AdCC-like pattern {19633533}. MYB immunoexpression alone does not equate with the diagnosis of AdCC; other adnexal tumours have also been found to significantly express MYB {28098399; 28323779}.
Identification of mutually exclusive MYB::NFIB or MYBL1::NFIB fusions may be helpful in selected cases.

Essential: coexistence of true small bilayered ducts (with or without secretion) and pseudocysts containing basophilic mucinous material in a multinodular neoplasm; two main cell types – ductal and myoepithelial cells.

Desirable: perineural invasion; coexpression of MYB and KIT (CD117); demonstration of MYB or MYBL1 rearrangements in selected cases.
Staging follows the eighth edition of the Union for International Cancer Control (UICC) TNM classification.

AdCC of the skin has a propensity for local recurrence, which has been reported to occur in > 50% of cases {3038974}. Rare cases metastasizing to regional lymph nodes or distant sites (lung, pleura, or liver) have been reported {10188691; 32618709}. Lesions located in the vulva may behave more aggressively, but larger studies are needed to validate this supposition. No statistically significant association has been found between tumour grade and local recurrence {24025525}. In a multivariate analysis of 451 cases, a more recent year of diagnosis, advanced patient age, and advanced stage were associated with poorer outcomes {32798575}.
